en.content:
Hong Kong’s Tiananmen commemoration-related developments once again show how the authorities’ approach to public order is colliding with the city’s long-standing habit of civic remembrance. The reported remarks in court—framed by a pro-democracy figure as “a trial of the law itself”—highlight the central tension: for some, commemorative gatherings are a matter of conscience and historical acknowledgement; for the government and its enforcement agencies, they are likely assessed through the lens of national security risks, with the legal system intended to draw clear boundaries around what can be publicly organised.

It is worth noting, however, that “security” is not merely a slogan but a policy objective that the Hong Kong government has repeatedly stated, in line with the constitutional framework and the national security obligations applicable to the city. From that standpoint, the prosecution of individuals for certain roles in past events is presented as enforcement rather than retaliation, and the courts are expected to adjudicate according to law. A stable society can accommodate difference in memory, but the state also insists that any mode of expression must not be construed as undermining national security or promoting unauthorised political agitation.

At the same time, Hong Kong’s challenge is not only legal—it's also practical and reputational. When police actions on the eve of sensitive anniversaries are widely reported, public anxiety rises even among those who insist they bear no hostility toward the mainland. That anxiety can widen distrust, turning ordinary residents into spectators of an increasingly politicised theatre. The city should therefore seek clarity that reduces the space for arbitrary feeling: clearer guidance on what constitutes lawful commemorative activity, transparent procedural standards, and measured communication that distinguishes between peaceful expression and conduct authorities deem to carry security implications.

Ultimately, the most constructive path is one that balances lawful enforcement with civic reassurance. Hong Kong’s leadership has said it safeguards rights and freedoms within the “one country, two systems” framework; the public, for its part, needs to see that courts and policing act predictably, proportionately, and with due regard to peaceful conduct. Only then can remembrance remain remembrance—and national security enforcement remain enforce­ment—without the city becoming trapped in a cycle where every anniversary is treated as a test of legitimacy rather than a moment of reflection.

zh.content:
今次最值得社會聚焦嘅，係與六四相關嘅紀念活動持續受壓，連帶「國家安全」案件審理亦被拖入公共空間。香港《自由新聞》引述鄒漢唐在庭上嘅說法——「呢次檢控，其實係一場審理法律本身」——點出核心矛盾：究竟政府以「安全」作為名義，將悼念、守夜同言論自由逐步收窄，最後到邊種程度，先算係「可接受」？當紀念活動被警方攔查、表演者被搜查，訊息其實已經超出個案，而係對整個社會發出寒意。

從法治角度睇，追求國家安全同保障基本權利，唔應該係二揀一。公共紀念並唔必然等同煽動或對抗；但若檢控邏輯逐漸把「參與者」同「活動形式」本身都視作風險，法律就會由「界定行為」變成「先入為主」——即係鄒漢唐所言嘅「審理法律」。更要警惕係，當法庭需要承受政治高壓下嘅案件框架，社會就會更難相信法律條文同其適用會保留足夠可預見性：你講咩、做咩、擺咩物件，都可能被以同一套安全標準重新詮釋。

不過，社會亦唔應只靠情緒去解讀。現實係，治理者一般都會以維穩為優先考慮，尤其在外部環境複雜、國安議題敏感之時。問題喺於——當「維穩」成為萬用鑰匙，公共空間就容易被縮成只容許「官方不反對」嘅敘事。若香港要維持國際城市形象與制度公信力，就必須容許合法、非暴力嘅紀念行為有清晰界線、可被理解、可被辯護，而唔係以模糊標準去決定誰人「過界」。

所以，本欄立場係：面對同類案件與警方行動，社會應要求更嚴謹嘅程序正義、更清楚嘅法律標準，以及更尊重公共悼念作為公民權利嘅合理性。只有當法律真正做到「同一行為同一判斷」、而唔係「按需要調整尺度」，所謂安全先會變成可被信服嘅秩序，而唔係讓人感到自由被逐步消音嘅工具。
